title: Simmons takes challenge of opponent’s residency to state Supreme Court
summary: A sitting state delegate is asking the state's highest court to overturn a lower court ruling that would allow his primary challenger to remain on the ballot despite apparently not currently meeting residency requirements.
content:
by Bryan P. Sears, Maryland Matters March 25, 2026

by Bryan P. Sears, Maryland Matters March 25, 2026

A sitting state delegate is asking the state’s highest court to overturn a lower court ruling that would allow his primary challenger to remain on the ballot despite apparently not currently meeting residency requirements.

An Anne Arundel County Circuit Court judge last week dismissed Del. Gary Simmons’ (D-Anne Arundel) lawsuit challenging the residency of John Dove, a Democratic candidate for Simmons’ House seat. An attorney for is asking the Supreme Court of Maryland to rule that the lower court erred.

“If the Circuit Court’s order stands, and a registered voter could not challenge a candidate’s residency for any reason until six months before the election, then there could never be time to challenge a candidate in time for the Board of Election to comply with its requirements to complete, print and mail ballots before the primary election,” said Robbie Leonard, the Towson attorney representing Simmons.

A hearing before the Supreme Court of Maryland is set for Monday. Attorneys for Dove are expected to file a response to the appeal this week before oral arguments are scheduled.

In the lawsuit filed earlier this month, Simmons alleged that Dove filed to run using an address in Gambrills, but that he actually lives in Pasadena.

Additionally, Simmons, through his attorney, argued Dove perjured himself by signing a change of address form for his voter registration that claimed he lived in Gambrills.

Residency challenge of an Anne Arundel County Democrat heads toward an appeal

Jill Carter, a former state senator and attorney for Dove, asked the circuit judge to dismiss Simmons’ case, arguing that Dove had six months from the date of the November general election to move into the address he claimed in election records.

Carter said her client has until May 3 to move into the district. The lawsuit is “untimely,” adding “there is precedent in Maryland, about courts deciding untimely issues or issues that are premature.”

Anne Arundel County Circuit Judge Robert J. Thompson agreed. He granted Carter’s request for a dismissal before hearing arguments on the underlying case.

But Thompson, in his decision from the bench, acknowledged that “no matter what I do, the Supreme Court will weigh in on this at some point.”

In the 12-page appeal on behalf of Simmons, Leonard argues that there is a “clearly a conflict” in the existing state election law that must be resolved by the courts.

“The language of the current law on certificates of candidacy require a person to use their current address – not the address in which they will reside at least six months from the election,” Leonard wrote in the appeal.

“Here, (Dove) believed that he needed to have an address in the district at the time of filing his Certificate of Candidacy. One week before he filed his Certificate of Candidacy, (Dove) found an address that he could use, where he did not yet reside, and changed his address with the Board of Elections,” Leonard said. “At that time, he committed perjury, and his Voter Registration Application and subsequent Certificate of Candidacy should be stricken.”
